html:
Schedules, events and monitors

The google_calendar skill owns live external Google Calendar operations separately from these durable smTO actions. It shares Google Workspace identity in Parameter Store but never imports Scheduler recurrence, creates internal schedule records or mirrors provider events. See Google Calendar.

The Schedules & Reminders skill (schedule) exposes schedule.create, schedule.inspect, schedule.update, schedule.cancel, schedule.delete, and schedule.trigger through the existing durable event store. Use action_type="notification" and prompt for exact reminder text. A successful creation finishes the current request immediately; the scheduler persists the notification without calling the model. The Agent UI notification inbox also shows reminders delivered while the browser was disconnected.

Timing uses the existing fields: once with interval_seconds for a relative delay, once with next_run_at for an ISO date/time, interval with interval_seconds for recurring intervals, or calendar with a daily, weekly, monthly or yearly recurrence and local time (HH:MM, Monday=0 through Sunday=6). timezone defaults to the user/runtime timezone; stored trigger timestamps resolve to UTC. Ambiguous/nonexistent absolute local times require an explicit offset. Calendar recurrence skips nonexistent DST times and uses the first occurrence of a repeated local time once.

One-shot reminders support delays from one second; recurring reminders support ten seconds. Offline one-shots fire once on return with late metadata. Recurring schedules deliver one coalesced late notification, then advance from the current time (calendar schedules advance to the next matching wall time), without replaying missed intervals. Reminder publication, its run receipt and schedule advancement share one transaction. The active Controller publishes that transaction in RAM and checkpoints it through the shared recovery owner. Standalone event stores use a SQLite write transaction. Concurrent claims cannot duplicate the same committed reminder; recovered state retains the recorded occurrence and launch identity. This does not make a RAM publication independently durable before the Controller's recovery protocol saves it.

Use the returned schedule_id (event_id remains an alias) to inspect or cancel. Cancellation preserves history and reports cancelled, already_cancelled, already_completed, or not_found. Creating schedules requires an active scheduler; discovery reports the actual store/worker availability.

Inspecting and counting schedules

schedule.inspect is an initial tool when permitted and the schedule store exists. It remains readable when the scheduler worker is offline or future execution is disabled. Capability exclusions still apply. Other management tools retain their existing execution prerequisites.

Call without an ID to list saved schedules; status="active" selects enabled schedules, while omission includes all non-deleted states. total_count and status_counts cover all matches; returned_count counts the displayed rows. included_statuses identifies the counted states. Zero counts establish no matches in those states now, not the absence of deleted schedules or historical activity. limit defaults to 20 and allows up to 100. complete=false means the displayed list was truncated. For count questions, set summary_only=true: the tool returns exact counts without rows and with complete=true, providing complete evidence for a count answer even when more than 100 schedules exist. A truncated listing cannot be cited as complete evidence; use the count-only view instead. scheduler.enabled and scheduler.worker_active describe execution readiness separately from saved status. Use one observed schedule_id with include_instruction or include_runs for details.

The current run's jobs, waits and task board are separate from saved schedules. Models must inspect schedules before reporting their count. Failed discovery or inspection means the count is unknown; an empty job list is not schedule evidence. If discovery is needed, use discover_tools({"skill_ids":["schedule"]}), then the advertised schedule__inspect function.

action_type="agent_prompt" retains the existing scheduled task queue and saved authorization/target scope for future Agent work, with its existing execution and recovery semantics. It requires inference at execution time. Use core wait_for_event for suspension and continuation of the current run, manage_job(wait) for an already running process, and Monitors for repeated condition checks. User-facing timers use schedules; ordinary program sleeps and explicitly requested OS cron/timer setup remain valid shell tasks.

For a timed wait in the current task, desktop and mobile show −, an adjustment amount and unit, +, and Wake now beside the countdown. The adjustment defaults to one minute; seconds and hours are also available. Changes update the saved deadline and survive refresh or restart. Subtracting all remaining time requests an immediate wake, just like Wake now. Wake requested · waiting to resume means the request is saved and the task will continue when execution capacity is available. These controls apply to timed sleeps; schedule, monitor, provider and job waits retain their existing controls. The adjacent Navigator button opens the Conversation Navigator to jump between prompts, including in short conversations.

Saved schedule definitions retain their captured operational scope and execution settings. At launch, the scheduled-event owner captures the current Controller model-routing snapshot for each new occurrence, including its selected connection and generation settings. Later routing changes therefore affect future occurrences; an accepted occurrence retains its own snapshot on resume. This does not rewrite the saved schedule's Gateway or permission scope. Notification-only reminders perform no inference. See scheduled model configuration.

monitor.start requires an actual command and deterministic settings from the model. monitor.inspect and monitor.stop operate on observed monitor IDs. The adapter does not draft a missing command. route_groups/monitor_service.py owns monitor manager initialization, and route_groups/monitors.py owns its routes.

An explicit Create Monitor workflow may call monitors/drafting.py. Configured deterministic conditions are evaluated mechanically; an explicitly configured judged/hybrid monitor may use the bounded condition judge at its configured cadence. Ordinary chat never invokes these helpers before the model.

The monitor guide describes execution modes, judge budgets, cooperative cancellation, history limits and recovery ownership.

Use actual event/monitor IDs for waits. Keep credentials out of stored prompts; services receive scoped runtime context.

Schedule ownership and recovery

Owner Responsibility
Creation and scope capture Validate action/timing and retain accepted policy, model settings, source references and Gateway intent.
Management service Share inspection, routine edits, cancellation, deletion and explicit triggering between HTTP and native tools.
Store factory and SQL adapter Select the live hub repository when the path has an owner; otherwise serve standalone SQL storage and shared patch validation.
RAM store Atomically publish definitions, due claims, reminder effects, occurrence ownership and inbox changes.
Record indexes Maintain source/temporal/occurrence uniqueness, due ordering, open runs and notification indexes in the same transaction.
Scheduler Poll eligible work and call an injected Agent launcher; reminder effects already exist when a claim returns.
Timing and models Validate recurrence patterns and resolve their next UTC occurrence.
Outcome projection Translate accepted native completion or open/waiting state into the occurrence record.
flowchart LR C[Validated creation and accepted scope] --> S[Schedule definition] S --> D[Atomic due claim] D --> R[Reminder and occurrence receipt] D --> Q[Agent launch callback] Q --> O[Owned execution occurrence] O --> T[Native outcome reconciliation] S --> H[Controller checkpoint and recovery] R --> H O --> H

AgentEventStore reuses a hub's event repository only for the same resolved path; a second path cannot silently replace it. Active RAM operations reject direct event SQL. Recovery loading initializes schema and rebuilds ordered indexes before normal operation. See Controller state for the shared checkpoint and recovery boundary.

A temporal request ID reconciles to its original record even after completion or deletion. Its anchored due time is checked only after reconciliation, so retrying an already committed reminder cannot create a new one or fail merely because the original time passed. Prompt scheduling separately keys canonical prompt text and reuses live active/paused definitions. Later instruction edits retain that original source key. Terminal definitions permit a new live prompt schedule.

The worker clamps its polling delay to 0.1–1 second, even when an older setting requests a slower interval. This is a polling bound, not a delivery deadline: claim work and launcher callbacks can take longer. Disabled workers claim nothing. The stop signal interrupts the between-tick wait, but cannot interrupt a callback already executing. A launcher exception is recorded and does not blindly replay the already claimed occurrence.

Queued, running, paused, waiting and blocked occurrences all prevent overlap. A conflicting due occurrence advances the schedule and records a skipped attempt; an optional skip notification identifies the blocker. occurrence_key deduplicates launch receipts, and only an unclaimed queued receipt can acquire a server generation. Recovery cannot claim the same uncertain launch again under a new generation. Definition completion means there is no next occurrence; it does not prove the last Agent task succeeded. Native success requires accepted completion evidence.

Calendar patterns support daily/weekly intervals, a day of month/year, or the first/second/third/fourth/last weekday of a month/year. Weeks start on Monday and series intervals anchor to their start date. End dates are inclusive; numbered ranges allow 1–10,000 occurrences and include scheduled instants missed while offline or paused. Nonexistent DST times are omitted from that count and repeated times count once. Absolute days clamp to the final day of a shorter month. An exhausted series cannot be resumed until its recurrence is changed. The schedule user guide explains the corresponding controls.

Inspection distinguishes complete counts from bounded displayed rows. Routine native edits cannot replace captured execution authority or introduce private macros. Cancelling/deleting a definition preserves open occurrences; it does not send a stop request to them. Bulk deletion re-resolves IDs inside the transaction and checks the reviewed membership digest. Metadata or active-run changes alone do not change that digest. The failed filter considers the five most recent attempts, and deletion previews show at most 100 rows.

Inbox read/dismissed state is independent of schedule and execution state. When notifications are disabled, newly recorded items remain as read with suppression metadata. Source-ID deduplication can reuse an existing item even if it was read or dismissed. Run retention defaults to 5,000 entries and only prunes older settled attempts; open work can exceed that count. Notification retention keeps the newest max(100, max_run_history) items without prioritizing unread entries. The notification architecture describes API projection, skill adapters and shared observer wakeups.

RAM event tests exercise rollback, contention, deletion and checkpoint restoration. Calendar tests cover month ends, leap days, DST and finite series; store tests cover standalone persistence and overlapping claims. These are isolated fixtures, not a guarantee of exact wall-clock delivery on a deployed host.

Schedule Manager browser flows

schedules.js owns the management page's cards, history, selection and confirmation dialogs. The shared editor owns form state; time and recurrence helpers format the server's saved definition. This browser controller does not calculate future occurrences or run Agent work. Its public event.context projection is read-only display information, never an edit payload. The user guide describes the controls.

flowchart TD API[Durable event API] --> Summaries[Definitions, five-run summaries and independent active runs] Summaries --> View[Local search, status filter and display sort] View --> Cards[Cached schedule cards and current-run links] Cards --> History[Expanded history pages of 30 runs] History --> API Cards --> Editor[Shared schedule editor] Editor --> Routine[Narrow creation or routine-edit request] Routine --> API Cards --> Actions[Pause, resume, trigger, cancel or delete controls] Actions --> API View --> Selection[Explicit IDs or all-matching query with exclusions] Selection --> Review[Server deletion preview and membership digest] Review --> Confirm[Explicit confirmation with reviewed digest] Confirm --> API Updates[Shared update stream, visibility and reconnect] --> Refresh[Coalesced refresh] Refresh --> API

Search matches loaded title, prompt and reminder text case-insensitively. Failed recently uses the fixed five-run summary, even when a longer history page is open. The independent active_runs map can identify an open occurrence outside that summary window. Display sort never changes selection membership. Search or filter changes cancel selection; filter and sort preferences are retained by the UI session helper. Explicit IDs and all-matching exclusions are each capped at 1,000 locally and in the server selection schema.

Refresh, history and presentation

The page subscribes to event, task and settings invalidations and uses a 100 ms timer to combine notifications. The timer skips its fetch when hidden, and becoming visible schedules another refresh. This does not cancel an already-running fetch. There is no continuous page polling loop.

sequenceDiagram participant Update as Update stream or page event participant UI as Schedule controller participant API as Event API participant Cards as Rendered cards Update->>UI: Invalidate UI->>UI: Coalesce for 100 ms and check visibility alt A list refresh is already running UI->>UI: Set refreshAgain and share its promise else Start refresh UI->>API: GET events with run_limit=5 API-->>UI: Definitions, summaries, active runs and enabled state UI->>UI: Prune obsolete selection/card IDs and update local state UI->>Cards: Reuse unchanged cards and restore replaced action focus loop Each expanded managed event UI->>API: GET runs with limit=30 at retained offset API-->>UI: History page or visible history error UI->>Cards: Update history panel end opt Another refresh was requested during the work UI->>UI: Repeat before releasing shared refresh promise end end

History requests are also shared per event. A concurrent request marks that history dirty; the existing request repeats while the panel remains expanded, using its original offset. A later offset does not replace that in-flight request's offset. List failures keep prior data visible and expose a page error; history failures preserve the cached page and offer a retry. A successful list refresh updates the cards without overwriting the editor's unsaved form.

Single actions have per-event busy guards. Status uses the narrow Manager PATCH; manual trigger uses POST. Cancel and delete use confirmation dialogs and separate lifecycle endpoints. Successful mutations refresh server facts. A card action error remains visible while the controller attempts that refresh. These controls change the definition or request an occurrence; stopping an already-started run belongs to that occurrence's normal task controls.

Reviewed bulk deletion

The browser captures either explicit IDs or a query/status plus exclusions when the dialog opens. The server preview determines candidate and active-run counts. The UI does not send public execution context, model settings or display sort. Closing or rereviewing the dialog advances a generation counter so an obsolete preview response cannot populate a newer review.

sequenceDiagram participant User participant UI as Schedule controller participant API as Manager API and Schedule service participant Store as Event store User->>UI: Delete selected schedules UI->>UI: Capture selection and preview generation UI->>API: POST delete-preview with selection API->>Store: Resolve current matching managed definitions Store-->>UI: Candidate count, active-run count and membership digest UI->>UI: Accept only newest response for an open dialog User->>UI: Confirm reviewed deletion UI->>API: POST bulk-delete with selection and digest API->>Store: Re-resolve and compare digest in one transaction alt Selected ID set changed Store-->>API: ScheduleSelectionChanged before mutation API-->>UI: HTTP 409 selection_changed UI->>UI: Disable confirmation and require another preview else Membership unchanged Store->>Store: Soft-delete definitions while retaining run receipts Store-->>API: Committed deletion and current active-run counts API-->>UI: Result UI->>UI: Clear selection, refresh and close dialog end

The selection contract hashes only the versioned sorted unique ID set. An explicit selection ignores missing, deleted or nonscheduled IDs. All-matching selection is resolved against current query/status membership again at commit. For the failed filter, the Schedule service first reconciles recent occurrence outcomes before both preview and confirmation. Metadata or active-run changes alone do not invalidate review, but a metadata change that moves an item into or out of the selected query does. The preview includes at most 100 summaries while its counts cover the complete selection.

The SQL store uses an immediate write transaction, and the RAM store uses its atomic repository transaction. A membership conflict or write failure leaves the whole deletion unapplied. Soft deletion retains occurrence receipts and does not cancel current runs. The browser treats any HTTP 409 as requiring a new review; other errors remain in the dialog without claiming success.

Manager tests exercise the matching window, independent active-run facts, selection limits, membership races, transaction rollback and retained occurrences with inference/launch work disabled. The source review also covers browser refresh and focus handling; those server fixtures do not prove every keyboard or browser timing interaction.

Shared schedule editor and prompt matching

schedule_editor.js provides the form used by Manager cards, Chat prompt actions and Workflow bindings. Each created dialog owns its fields and loaded-form baseline. The prompt_schedule.js adapter owns source lookup and calendar-button state. The page's cached cards, the open draft and the server's definition remain separate states.

flowchart TD Manager[Manager card or New schedule] --> Form[Shared editor and loaded baseline] Prompt[Chat draft or historical prompt] --> Lookup[Server prompt-match lookup] Lookup --> Form Workflow[Reviewed Workflow revision] --> Form Form --> Values[Literal prompt, name and timing choices] Values --> Timing[Structured timing payload] Timing --> Intent{Save source?} Intent -->|New Manager definition| Create[Action and timing creation request] Intent -->|New prompt source| Source[Captured prompt and source request identity] Intent -->|Existing definition| Patch[Changed routine fields only] Intent -->|Workflow callback| Binding[Revision-bound recipe schedule intent] Create --> API[Existing server validation and storage] Source --> API Patch --> API Binding --> API API --> Definition[Saved definition and next trigger] Definition --> Occurrence[Later ordinary occurrence execution]

Opening clones a supplied definition, resets the form and initializes timing in the saved series timezone. New Manager definitions default to daily; new prompt sources default to once. A new source prompt is read-only, while an existing schedule's instruction can be edited. Type is fixed for existing definitions and hidden for prompt/Workflow sources. Existing public execution context is displayed but never copied into an edit payload.

Prompt matching and invalidation

Calendar buttons are attached only to eligible ordinary prompt text. User-authored turn actions read the current request identity and text when clicked. Hover/focus warms a lookup, while opening the editor forces a server lookup and captures the composer's execution choices before awaiting it. Saving an unsent draft does not send or clear the Chat composer.

sequenceDiagram actor U as Human participant P as Prompt adapter participant C as Local normalized cache participant A as Prompt-schedule API participant E as Shared editor U->>P: Focus calendar or request editor P->>C: Normalize NFC, line endings and outer whitespace alt Cached lookup and no forced refresh C-->>P: Saved presentation result else New or forced lookup P->>P: Share pending request for the same normalized key P->>A: POST prompt-schedule/resolve A-->>P: Existing definition or no match, suggested title alt Lookup generation changed P->>P: Resolve again in the current generation else Generation still current P->>C: Cache result and repaint matching mounted buttons end end opt Explicit open succeeds P->>E: Definition or source prompt with captured choices E-->>U: Review editable schedule end Note over P,A: Lookup does not create a definition or execute a task

The adapter coalesces requests by normalized prompt. An events.changed signal advances its generation, clears presentation cache and resets mounted buttons. Previously known scheduled prompts are resolved again; untouched unscheduled buttons remain lazy. A response from an older generation triggers another lookup before adoption. Detached buttons are pruned when the registry is visited. The adapter and subscriptions have document lifetime and expose no disposal hook.

The server owns source identity and concurrent-create deduplication. Its prompt boundary uses canonical text: NFC, normalized line endings and trimmed outer whitespace. Case and internal indentation remain distinct. Lookup rejects application commands, empty/oversized text and private macro syntax. Literal strings that resemble credentials are accepted as prompt text; the current boundary does not apply a credential-content rejection rule. The route handlers resolve existing identity before applying new-definition defaults, allowing another tab's accepted definition to be returned as outcome: existing.

Form encoding and timezone boundaries

schedule_recurrence.js encodes the selected fields; schedule_time.js formats timestamps and wall times. Neither owns timers, network calls or recurrence arithmetic. A local summary is not proof that the server will accept the timing.

Choice Wire representation Authority retained by the server
Once Local date/time string plus timezone. Future-time validation and conversion to an absolute trigger.
Interval Numeric value multiplied by its seconds unit; optional explicit first date/time. Interval bounds and preservation or initialization of the next trigger.
Calendar Frequency/pattern, interval, start date, wall time, selected weekdays and finite range. Calendar validity, DST resolution and future occurrence calculation.

Weekdays encodes weekly interval one with Monday–Friday indices. Monthly/yearly choices encode absolute day or relative weekday patterns. Finite ranges contain an end date or occurrence count. Formatting names a numbered range's scheduled occurrences; it does not reinterpret them as successful executions.

The editor trims name and timezone but leaves prompt text for server normalization. It computes changes against the loaded form. Existing definitions receive only changed name, instruction and timing fields; changing schedule type sends the full new timing shape. An unchecked interval start omits next_run_at. These routine PATCHes carry no browser revision precondition and do not submit public context, model configuration or permission policy. Concurrent field edits remain subject to the server's existing update behavior.

For a new prompt source, the client sends the captured source prompt, request ID, integrity-setting override and optional Gateway intent. Other displayed execution fields are not an authority payload. Workflow scheduling delegates to its supplied save callback, which pins the reviewed recipe revision as described in Workflow browser flows.

Save acknowledgement, duplicate matches and focus

sequenceDiagram actor U as Human participant E as Shared editor participant A as Selected API or caller save callback participant O as Caller refresh and event observers U->>E: Save or Resume E->>E: Check enabled/busy state and required form choices E->>E: Build routine payload and add active status for Resume E->>A: Explicit create, PATCH or Workflow binding request alt Request rejected or unconfirmed A-->>E: Error E-->>U: Keep draft and show feedback else Server acknowledges A-->>E: Saved or existing definition E->>O: Await onSaved callback alt Callback succeeds E->>O: Publish schedule-saved event alt Another tab already created this prompt schedule E-->>U: Reopen existing definition and explain the match else Ordinary save E-->>U: Close and restore focus end else Callback fails after acknowledgement O-->>E: Error E-->>U: Show error without undoing the saved definition end end E->>E: Release busy state and recompute save availability

The editor prevents duplicate submissions and disables Save while saving, when scheduling is disabled or when an existing form has no changes. Resume adds active status after normal validity checks. Save chooses /events/manager, the prompt-schedule creation route, an existing definition's Manager PATCH, or a caller supplied Workflow save callback. Future execution remains owned by the scheduler.

User close buttons, Escape and native dialog cancellation are blocked while saving. Tab navigation wraps through visible enabled controls. After close, focus returns to the original control if connected, a replacement card action with the same identity, or New schedule. Background inventory refresh does not reset the open form. The public open() method itself has no pending-save guard or generation fence; callers must not assume that replacing a dialog cancels its request or suppresses all late feedback. There is no editor-owned request abort or teardown API.

This review covers all four browser modules. Server prompt normalization and the resolve/create boundary were inspected to correct the obsolete credential-rejection claim. Broader scheduling, scope capture and execution retain their separate evidence in this guide. Selected tests use isolated local stores and disabled task launching.

From a saved definition to an occurrence

The Controller separates three identities: the schedule definition, one scheduled occurrence and the task/attempt that executes it. A reminder has an occurrence and inbox item but needs no Agent task. The following sequences expand the ownership map above; ordinary execution continues through the task coordinator.

sequenceDiagram participant U as Manager or prompt-schedule caller participant A as Schedule HTTP adapter participant P as Controller policy and target owners participant D as Schedule domain participant S as Event store U->>A: Submit prompt, action and timing A->>A: Check enabled state and accepted product terms opt Prompt-schedule request A->>S: Resolve canonical prompt identity first S-->>A: Existing live definition or creation callback opt Existing live definition found A-->>U: Return existing definition end end opt A new definition is needed A->>P: Capture permission, capability and operational defaults P-->>A: Accepted scope and selected Gateway intent A->>D: Validate explicit timing and allowlisted scope D->>S: Publish definition and source identity S-->>U: Saved definition and next due time end Note over A,S: No command or model decision executes as a consequence of saving

schedule_manager.py constructs narrow request schemas from the domain's typed fields. Routine edits cannot write captured authority. The prompt-schedule path checks for an existing live definition before resolving creation defaults, so reopening it does not depend on the original Gateway still being available. New Agent schedules require an explicit selection or an enabled default Gateway. Permission capture reads the permission authority, rather than inferring it from legacy runtime controls.

Reminder delivery

sequenceDiagram participant W as Scheduler tick participant S as RAM event store participant H as Shared state transaction participant N as Notification readers W->>W: Check enabled state and reconcile earlier occurrences W->>S: Claim bounded due window using one current timestamp S->>H: Check open occurrence and advance recurrence alt Earlier occurrence still blocks this schedule S->>H: Insert skipped receipt and optional skip notification else Notification action is eligible S->>H: Insert completed reminder receipt and inbox item S->>H: Save next due time, counters and lateness metadata end H-->>S: Publish all changes together S-->>W: Claimed reminder already delivered N->>S: Read inbox and occurrence history S-->>N: Retained records, including offline delivery Note over W,N: No model call or Agent launcher is required

The atomic block is the store's publication boundary. The Controller's recovery checkpoint follows the shared state contract; the diagram is not a separate disk-save acknowledgement. A standalone store uses its SQL transaction. An interval schedule coalesces missed intervals into one delivery and computes its next time from the claim timestamp. Calendar advancement and finite-series counts remain owned by the recurrence functions. An open occurrence produces a skipped receipt while the definition advances; it does not start a second execution.

Scheduled Agent work

sequenceDiagram participant W as Scheduler or explicit trigger participant L as Scheduled-event launcher participant S as Event store participant C as Conversation and scope owners participant T as Task owner participant R as Ordinary request runtime W->>L: Launch accepted event and occurrence time L->>S: Create or reuse keyed queued occurrence L->>S: Claim occurrence for this server generation alt Already linked, settled or claimed S-->>L: Return existing occurrence without a new launch else Claim acquired L->>L: Check product terms before target resolution L->>C: Create stable occurrence conversation and request identities L->>C: Resolve saved target, policy and parameter references opt Saved-request Workflow L->>C: Validate pinned revision and materialize saved context end L->>C: Capture current Controller model route for this occurrence L->>T: Create queued or parameter-held task with accepted context T-->>L: Task identity and admission state L->>S: Link task to occurrence L->>T: Record usage and queue or start accepted task T->>R: Dispatch when all admission conditions permit R-->>S: Reconcile native outcome through event owner end

ScheduleService uses a deterministic occurrence key for automatic launches and a fresh key for each explicit manual trigger. The launch claim is separate from definition advancement and from task creation. Conversation, workflow, task, usage and outcome writes are also separate steps. If a callback fails, earlier accepted state may already exist; the scheduler records the failure and does not blindly repeat the claimed action.

Missing product-term acceptance consumes the claimed occurrence as skipped before creating its execution conversation. A scope-resolution failure records a failed occurrence and conversation result. Later failures have their own owners; the launcher does not promise to roll back all preceding writes. Saved operational authority remains captured, while a new occurrence takes the current model-routing snapshot. Resume retains that occurrence's accepted request identity.

Recovery and outcome reconciliation

flowchart TD Open[Read open occurrence index] --> Startup{Startup recovery?} Startup -->|Keyed occurrence lacks conversation| Prepare[Restore stable execution conversation identity] Startup -->|Existing execution conversation| Evidence[Read native summary, ownership and trace summary] Prepare --> Evidence Startup -->|Ordinary tick with execution conversation| Evidence Startup -->|Legacy record without conversation| Legacy[Use retained legacy task and continuation reconciliation] Evidence --> Orphan{Startup, no owner, queued or running, and absent or running native state?} Orphan -->|Yes| Interrupt[Mark occurrence and available projections interrupted; preserve effect evidence] Orphan -->|No| Missing{No native or trace evidence?} Missing -->|Yes| Keep[Keep current occurrence; live preparation is not completion] Missing -->|No| Outcome[Map native outcome, including completion acceptance] Outcome -->|Open wait or work| Wait[Retain open occurrence and prevent overlap] Outcome -->|Settled| Final[Finalize receipt, applicable notification and conversation projection]

event_shared.py reconciles current execution occurrences before normal workers resume at startup. It marks orphaned queued/running work interrupted without replaying commands. A claimed occurrence cannot acquire a second generation simply because a process disappeared. An ordinary live-process read with no native or trace evidence leaves preparation alone. Older records without execution-conversation identity retain their separate compatibility path.

execution_outcome requires accepted native completion for native answered/completed status; otherwise it projects partial. Confirmation, input, job, event, budget and resource waits stay open. Finalization ignores a stale parent trace after the occurrence has moved to a child request. Notification publication and occurrence/conversation projection are separate writes here; the reminder transaction above has a different boundary.

Monitor command execution and condition-trigger sequences are documented in Monitor workers and trigger flow.

Monitoring snapshot on scheduled work

Scheduled/event work captures the disabled-Agent-Check monitoring preference with its accepted scope. Updates retain the existing accepted value and dispatch carries it into the run. Missing legacy event scope values mean OFF. This preference adds optional Activity diagnostics only; it creates no new scheduled action, poll, model call or event trigger.
